patient.name: Raymond Kowalski
patient.chief_complaint: One year of progressive weakness and numbness in hands and feet, difficulty climbing stairs
patient.hpi: Raymond Kowalski is a 55-year-old retired postal supervisor who presents with a 12-month history of gradually worsening numbness, tingling, and weakness affecting all four extremities. The symptoms began insidiously with bilateral foot numbness described as a 'constant sock feeling,' but over the subsequent months he noticed progressive weakness in his legs, particularly difficulty rising from low chairs, climbing stairs, and walking more than two blocks. His hands became involved about 6 months ago with numbness and grip weakness affecting his ability to open jars and button his shirt. He has fallen twice in the past 4 months. He denies bowel or bladder dysfunction. He notes that his symptoms seem to fluctuate — some weeks feeling slightly better before worsening again — which he initially attributed to activity level. He was evaluated by his primary care physician who noted his HbA1c at 6.1% (prediabetic range) and wondered if this explained his symptoms, but his neurologist is less convinced this fully accounts for the proximal weakness. He has no recent viral illness, vaccination, or new medication prior to symptom onset. He denies alcohol use beyond occasional beer (less than 1 drink per week). Family history includes a paternal aunt with 'some kind of nerve problem' (details unknown). He is otherwise independent in activities of daily living though increasingly struggling.
patient.review_of_systems: Positive: leg and hand weakness, bilateral extremity numbness, unsteady gait, two falls, grip weakness. Negative: bowel/bladder dysfunction, visual changes, diplopia, dysphagia, shortness of breath, rash.

family_history: Father: hypertension, died MI age 71. Mother: type 2 diabetes, died stroke age 78. Paternal aunt: unspecified 'nerve problem' (details unknown).

social_history.note: Retired postal supervisor, married, 2 adult children. Former smoker (20 pack-years, quit age 48). Rare alcohol (less than 1 drink per week). No illicit drug use. Lives in two-story home.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. MMSE 29/30 (missed 1 recall). Normal language and cognition.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II-XII intact. No facial asymmetry. Normal extraocular movements. Normal facial sensation.
neurological_exam.motor: Mild proximal weakness: hip flexors 4/5 bilaterally, hip abductors 4/5 bilaterally, knee extensors 4+/5 bilaterally. Distal weakness: dorsiflexion 4/5 bilaterally, plantar flexion 4+/5 bilaterally. Hand intrinsics 4/5 bilaterally, grip strength mildly reduced. Upper extremity proximal strength 4+/5 bilateral deltoids and biceps.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reduced light touch and pinprick in glove-and-stocking distribution to mid-shin bilaterally and to wrists bilaterally. Vibration reduced at great toes (5 seconds) and ankles (8 seconds). Reduced proprioception at great toes bilaterally.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 1+ bilaterally, triceps 1+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 1+ bilaterally, patellar absent bilaterally, Achilles absent bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Mild dysmetria on finger-nose bilaterally. Heel-shin intact. Romberg positive.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, steppage gait. Tandem walking impaired. Unable to walk on heels. Toe walking mildly impaired.
neurological_exam.special_tests: Positive Romberg. No Babinski. No clonus. Tinel's sign negative at wrist bilaterally.

labs.interpretation: Abnormal values: Glucose 108 mg/dL (H), HbA1c 6.1 % (H), Fasting Glucose 108 mg/dL (H), Vitamin B12 248 pg/mL (H), ESR 32 mm/hr (H), Anti-sulfatide IgM Weakly positive (titer 1:100)  (H).

report.summary: ABNORMAL NCS/EMG. Mixed demyelinating and axonal features. Pattern is not classic pure axonal diabetic neuropathy nor classic CIDP. Most consistent with superimposed CIDP on a background of mild diabetic axonal neuropathy, or early CIDP. Further evaluation with CSF recommended.

motor.note: Mild velocity slowing proximal; no clear conduction block

motor.flag: prolonged DML, markedly slow velocity, reduced amplitude

muscles_tested.morphology: polyphasic MUPs, mildly long duration — proximal involvement

emg.summary: Denervation with chronic reinnervation in distal leg muscles. Proximal muscle (vastus lateralis) mildly involved — atypical for pure diabetic axonal pattern. Upper extremity distal involvement.

report.overall_impression: MIXED DEMYELINATING AND AXONAL PATTERN. Conduction velocities are slowed beyond what would be expected for typical diabetic axonal neuropathy (which preferentially reduces amplitudes rather than velocities). DMLs prolonged in upper and lower limbs. F-waves markedly prolonged in lower limbs. No unequivocal conduction block. Mild proximal EMG involvement. Pattern raises possibility of superimposed CIDP on prediabetic/early diabetic neuropathy, or early CIDP mimicking diabetic neuropathy. CSF protein analysis and consideration of nerve biopsy recommended.

output.procedure: Lumbar puncture at L3-L4, atraumatic technique

output.interpretation: Abnormal values: Methylmalonic Acid (MMA) 0.28 umol/L (H), Homocysteine 14.2 umol/L (H), Vitamin B12 (repeat) 244 pg/mL (H).

report.summary: Sural nerve biopsy: segmental demyelination and remyelination with onion bulb formation. Sparse perivascular mononuclear inflammatory infiltrates. No vasculitis. No amyloid deposits. Findings consistent with chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP).
report.histology: Semi-thin sections show 40% of fibers with segmental demyelination. Teased fiber preparation confirms demyelination-remyelination. Electron microscopy: onion bulb formations (12% of large fibers). Perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates in endoneurium. No necrotizing vasculitis. Congo red negative (no amyloid). PMP22: normal gene dosage by FISH.
report.interpretation: CIDP — inflammatory demyelinating neuropathy confirmed histologically. Prediabetes may contribute mild background axonal component but CIDP is the primary and treatable diagnosis.

output.interpretation: Abnormal values: Anti-sulfatide IgM (repeat) 1:100 weakly positive  (H).

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (CIDP) with background prediabetic neuropathy
critical_actions: Check serum IgA before IVIG — IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies is a contraindication
Perform LP for CSF protein to confirm CIDP diagnosis before long-term immunotherapy
Check anti-NF155/CNTN1 antibodies — nodopathy variants may not respond to IVIG
Initiate IVIG 2 g/kg induction — first-line evidence-based treatment for CIDP
Do not attribute all findings to prediabetes — demyelinating pattern requires separate explanation
contraindicated_actions: Do not start IVIG without checking serum IgA (risk of anaphylaxis in IgA deficiency)
Do not dismiss as pure diabetic neuropathy — demyelinating velocities and CSF protein require CIDP workup
Do not use rituximab as first-line — anti-MAG neuropathy (primary rituximab indication) has been excluded
Do not prescribe only symptomatic gabapentin/duloxetine without addressing underlying treatable CIDP

differential.key_distinguishing: HbA1c only 6.1% prediabetic; diabetic neuropathy would show length-dependent axonal pattern (amplitude loss > velocity slowing); demyelinating velocities and CSF dissociation not explained by prediabetes
No M-spike on SPEP; anti-MAG antibody not tested here but anti-sulfatide only weakly positive; no IgM paraprotein; terminal slowing pattern not present

Family history of paternal aunt with nerve problem is a red herring; CMT1 shows very slow uniform velocities <38 m/s throughout; onset age 55 is late; PMP22 on nerve biopsy was normal; CMT does not fluctuate
ESR mildly elevated 32 mm/hr but ANCA/ANA negative; vasculitic neuropathy typically asymmetric multifocal (mononeuritis multiplex); nerve biopsy showed no vasculitis

key_reasoning_points: MODERATE DIFFICULTY: Prediabetes (HbA1c 6.1%) creates diagnostic anchoring trap — easy to attribute to diabetes and miss treatable CIDP
Key discriminator: NCS velocities are too slow for pure axonal diabetic neuropathy (which reduces amplitudes more than velocities)
Proximal muscle EMG involvement (vastus lateralis) is a red flag for pure distal diabetic neuropathy
CSF albumino-cytologic dissociation (protein 94 mg/dL, 2 WBC) clinches CIDP diagnosis
Fluctuating symptom course is classic for CIDP (relapsing-remitting pattern)
Weakly positive anti-sulfatide IgM (1:100) is a distractor — clinically significant anti-sulfatide neuropathy requires high titers with IgM paraprotein
IVIG is first-line for CIDP; checking IgA first is mandatory safety step
Anti-NF155+ nodopathy variant is typically refractory to IVIG — important to exclude
